How did The Masters Apprentices get their name?

Jim Keays explained it best in his autobiography His Master's Voice:

“...seemingly out of nowhere, Mick suggested Masters Apprentices, explaining we were apprentices to the masters of blues – Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley, Jimmy Reed, Elmore James, Robert Johnson, among others.”

Jim later reflected:

“It was very much Mick’s band, he was the leader... we accepted his suggestion and in later years I thought it was an inspired choice.”

More than 60 years later, that inspired choice remains one of the most recognisable names in Australian rock history.

🫣‼️One challenge I face every month is creating a table with genuinely diverse opinions. It would be much easier if I simply gathered 12 people who already agreed with each other for June’s discussion on abortion.

But I do not want a homogenized table. That’s the challenge and beauty of trying to build authentic community.

So I’m trying something a little different.

If you RSVP, it would actually help to know your perspective via DM. If too many people land on one side of the discussion, I may save seats to help balance the table. Maybe you’re strongly pro-life, strongly pro-choice, somewhere in the middle, conflicted, or honestly undecided. All of that matters.

Right now, there are already people RSVP’d from different camps of thought, but I’m especially looking to balance the scale with more pro-choice voices, mixed views, and undecided perspectives.

If that’s you, and you’d enjoy a free drink, some food, and a safe place for honest discussion, send me an RSVP.

No shouting matches.
No humiliation.
No pressure.
Just real people having a real conversation about something that deeply impacts human lives.

Ohhh… and one more thing 👀

For July’s Table Talk, I’ll have a videographer capturing parts of the evening to help model something our culture desperately needs right now: how to have meaningful conversations with people we disagree with. 😮😮

You might actually help teach people across the country what respectful discourse can look like.

Heat pump water heaters have been around for over a decade. If you follow this channel, you probably know they're three to five times more efficient than a standard electric tank. Maybe you've got one. I do. But here's what most people don't realize. Even if you own a heat pump water heater, it's still pretty dumb. It heats reactively. The tank drops below the setpoint, the compressor kicks on. It doesn't know your schedule. It doesn't know your electricity rates. And it definitely doesn't know when your solar panels are cranking. Two Boston startups think that's a massive missed opportunity. They're treating the water heater as a thermal battery, a cheap, insulated vessel that can store energy as heat, shift electricity use to cheaper hours, and participate in grid services. One of them, Wilmington, Massachusetts-based Cala Systems, invited me to tour their factory. Their predictive software is licensed from the National Renewable Energy Lab. According to a California Energy Commission study, intelligent scheduling on time-of-use rate plans alone can cut costs by 15 to 19 percent beyond what a standard heat pump water heater already saves. So I went inside to find out: is a smart water heater actually worth the premium? Or is "intelligent" just a buzzword bumper sticker slapped on a tank of hot water?

I was a teenager on a cruise when I first saw ocean pollution up close. Late at night, I saw crew dumping garbage into the ocean. A stream of trash stretching off toward the horizon. But that garbage spilling into the ocean was just the tip of the trashberg. And that trashberg… is mainly plastic. Plastic makes up about 80 percent of marine pollution. And it doesn't always come from where you'd expect. Most people think of waste plastic as straws, bottles, and grocery bags washing off beaches. But when a Dutch nonprofit called The Ocean Cleanup sailed out to the Great Pacific Garbage Patch to scoop it all up… they found something else entirely. More than three-quarters of the plastic wasn’t consumer trash... at all. It didn’t even come from the shore! Even worse, cleaning it up was a lot harder than anyone hoped. So, they did something surprising. They turned around, returned to shore, and started tackling the plastic problem upstream. This is the story of what The Ocean Cleanup discovered once they started studying the problem up close… and why solving ocean plastic might mean turning off the tap, and not just mopping up what's already spilled.

👉 “Undecided” = Instant Rejection at Top Schools?

❌ Nope. Big myth.

👉 In many top U.S. & European universities, students are allowed to enter without choosing a major for the first 1–2 years.

✨ That’s called Undecided / Undeclared.

💡 What “Undecided” REALLY means
• You’re exploring before locking in a lifelong path
• You’re taking general courses and discovering your strengths
• You’re using a flexible education system (not wasting time)

📊 Fun fact:
🔹 20–50% of U.S. students start Undecided
🔹 ~75% change their major at least once anyway

😰 Common fears (and the truth)
❌ “Undecided students get rejected more” → False
❌ “Top universities don’t like it” → False
❌ “It means no goals” → False

✅ Universities care more about:
• Curiosity
• Academic effort
• Growth mindset
—not whether you picked a major at 17.

⚠️ When Undecided may NOT be ideal
• Highly competitive majors (Engineering, Business, Nursing)
• Schools that require major selection from Year 1

👉 In these cases:
Apply with a major → transfer internally later

🎯 Smart strategy
✔️ Ivy League / Liberal Arts schools → Undecided is OK
✔️ STEM-heavy schools → Choose a clear major
✔️ Essays matter more than the label

✨ Not knowing your major yet ≠ not knowing your future.
Exploration is a strength—when done strategically.

What if you could power cities just by mixing river water with seawater? Around 15,000 TWh of energy pours into the oceans each year as freshwater blends with saltwater at river mouths. That amounts to roughly half the energy the world consumes in electricity every year. And we may have finally found a way to tap it. It’s called osmotic power, and it could provide clean energy around the clock. As freshwater becomes scarcer, more cities are turning to desalination plants to meet their water needs. Desalination is energy-intensive, but osmotic power could use the same salty wastewater from desalination to generate electricity instead of just dumping it back in the ocean. But how does this tech work? Could a combination of fresh and saltwater be the “solution” to the world’s ever-increasing energy demands?

And in France, an enzymatic recycling plant is transforming previously unrecyclable polyester textiles back into virgin-quality plastic feedstock. We've been sold the recycling dream for decades, but the reality? Most plastic still ends up in landfills or the ocean. Could these breakthroughs finally turn recycling from marketing lie into working reality?

So I did a post a while back about the kind of wedding we wanted because honestly, I was so torn. After a big heart-to-heart, we’ve decided we want the full traditional wedding day experience. Cue the venue hunt... and after visiting seven places, we’ve narrowed it down to two. 

One venue completely stole our hearts. It ticks every box and we fell in love with it instantly. The other is also gorgeous and ticks most of our boxes and it’s not as expensive. 

Here’s the dilemma:  
The venue we love is further away for our families, has no on-site parking, and most photo spots are outdoors (so we’re praying for good weather but it is Scotland...). It includes stunning accommodation for both bridal and groom parties the night before, with separate sleeping areas so we won’t see each other before the ceremony. It’s popular, hard to book, and honestly feels special. 

The second venue is closer for everyone, has more indoor photo options, and the staff are lovely. But the main room has pillars I find annoying, the gardens overlook a residential area, and it’s right off a busy road with no gate. It doesn’t offer pre-wedding accommodation, but it would save us a good chunk of money we could put toward the honeymoon. 

Both are beautiful. Both are expensive. We just don’t want to have any regrets.

Gene McNeely was a legend.

I first met Gene in 2004 at EAA/Oshkosh, introduced by a friend who also lived at Spruce Creek. At the time, Gene was flying with the famous Aeroshell Aerobatic Team, and I was starstruck—blushing and fumbling over my words like a drunken schoolgirl as I shook his hand. But Gene’s warm smile and welcoming hug immediately put me at ease. From that first handshake, I felt like part of the airshow family—and that feeling never changed. Every time I saw him—at Oshkosh, Sun 'n Fun, the Reno Air Races, or at his home in Spruce Creek—he greeted me the same way:

"Kandi!" he’d yell as a smile appeared on his face.
"How you doin’, girl? How’s the jet sellin’ business?" And then came the hug.

I loved hearing his stories. On a recent visit to Spruce Creek, Gene told me about walking around Oshkosh in the 1980s with his young son, Greg. Awestruck by the airplanes and airshow performers, he turned to Greg and said, "I'm going to fly airshows here someday, son." And by God… he did.

Gene flew with the Aeroshell team at EAA AirVenture until retiring in 2017. (Read his retirement story here: https://www.eaa.org/airventure/eaa-airventure-news-and-multimedia/eaa-airventure-news/eaa-airventure-oshkosh/07-27-2018-mcneely-not-really-retired-at-all).

Gene will be missed by many. But more importantly, he left an indelible mark on generations of aviators and aviatrixes alike—including me. His joy being in the air and around airplanes was contagious, and I hope to carry forward his tradition of sharing that passion with future generations.

Because life is better with airplanes in it. 

Godspeed, Gene.  Enjoy your eternal flight.

Sodium-ion battery technology isn’t exactly new, but something interesting is happening. CATL, the world’s biggest lithium battery manufacturer, says that up to half the market could switch to sodium. That’s right—the biggest name in lithium batteries is betting against lithium. Looks like lithium might need to recharge its reputation. After all, sodium-ion batteries are nearly as good lithium, and salt is much cheaper and easier to access than lithium. It’s been a full year since I installed these solar panels and a large home battery on my new house … and I’ve got some news. They say solar power can save you thousands on energy bills, but what actually happened. This past year was a bit of a rollercoaster ride from the challenges of getting them installed to seeing how well they handled powering my all-electric house through heat waves, freezing temperatures, and a couple of small power outages. Spoiler alert: solar isn’t all sunshine and rainbows.  Was my net zero house ready for all of it?  Was I able to achieve net zero energy?  And most important … was it worth it? Let’s just say, I learned some pretty surprising lessons that may be of use to you.

Has anyone asked you what you want to major in when you attend college? Don’t be afraid or concerned to be applying to college without declaring a major. It may be the right choice for you, but before you choose to do so, let’s review what it means to be undecided and some of the advantages and disadvantages of applying this way.
